Chapter Eight: The Ties That Bind—Family, Memory, and the Cost of Escape.
Leaving North Korea? It's never just about one person making a choice.
Every escape sets off a ripple through a web of relationships—parents, siblings, friends. And the truth is, those left behind often pay a steep price for the decisions of one.
That guilt... it’s a heavy burden. And the longing for connection? It never really fades.
Imagine a woman who’s finally made it to South Korea. Most evenings, she just sits by her phone, staring at it, hoping for some word from home. She knows every call, every message, could put her family in danger—yet she can’t help herself. Letting go feels impossible.
So she sends money through secret channels, taking the risk each time, just for the chance that help will reach the people she loves.
For some, the pain of separation is almost too much to bear. Think of a father who couldn’t bring his children with him.
He’s haunted by their faces, dreaming of reunion, even though he knows it might never happen. The ache of absence shapes every single day, every decision he makes.
But the cost of escape? It’s not just emotional—it’s practical, too.
Many defectors struggle to find work or build stable lives. Supporting themselves, and those left behind, becomes a daily pressure that just doesn’t let up.
Some manage to succeed, creating new families and tight-knit communities. But others? They get crushed under the weight of all that expectation.
And then, there’s memory.
Sometimes it’s a comfort—a reminder of kindness and strength. Other times, it’s a curse.
Picture a young man, trying to start over. But he can’t forget his friends back home. Are they okay? Do they blame him for leaving? Do they even understand why he had to go?
Most people have no idea how hard it is to start fresh. The past is always there, shaping every hope, every fear, every dream.
But here’s something important—amid all that longing and regret, there’s real resilience. The bonds of family and memory? They’re not easily broken.
They endure—even across borders, even after years apart.
